steps.intent: The United States' primary objective is to maintain Council consensus on the counter-terrorism architecture by extending the mandate of the 1988 Sanctions Monitoring Team for 12 months, ensuring vital independent reporting on the growing external threat posed by ISIL-K and Al-Qaeda emanating from Afghanistan. The most difficult points during negotiations will involve pushback from the Russian Federation and China regarding references to the Taliban's human rights abuses—especially against women and girls—and calls to soften language on Taliban obligations, as well as sensitive regional security concerns raised by incoming member Pakistan regarding cross-border militant operations. By anchoring the text firmly in the established mandate of Resolution 2763 (2024) while addressing heightened transnational terror risks, the draft is calibrated to secure unanimous or broad adoption without triggering a veto.

Requests the Monitoring Team to actively track and report on the evolving regional and transnational threat posed by terrorist groups operating in or from Afghanistan, notably ISIL-K, Al-Qaida, and the East Turkestan Islamic Movement (ETIM), including foreign terrorist fighters and their networks, recruitment, and financing mechanisms;

Requests the Monitoring Team to continue to cooperate closely with the United Nations Assistance Mission in Afghanistan (UNAMA) and relevant United Nations counter-terrorism bodies and sanctions committees, and encourages the Monitoring Team to strengthen its engagement with the Afghan interim Administration, including through visits to Afghanistan;

Reaffirming the importance of addressing Afghanistan's dire economic and humanitarian challenges, restoring its banking and financial system, and creating conditions for sustainable economic development,

messages.Algeria: Algeria supports the renewal of the Analytical Support and Sanctions Monitoring Team mandate to ensure the continued effectiveness of the sanctions regime against terrorist threats in Afghanistan. We believe it is essential to reaffirm that listing and delisting processes remain Member State-driven and that the Monitoring Team operates in an independent, objective, and non-politicized manner. We stand ready to work constructively with the penholder to reach a swift consensus on the draft.
messages.China: China supports the renewal of the Monitoring Team's mandate to support the 1988 Committee, but the text must take a comprehensive and balanced approach to counter-terrorism. The resolution must explicitly address all terrorist groups threatening regional security, particularly the East Turkestan Islamic Movement (ETIM), which poses a direct security threat to China and the region. Furthermore, the Monitoring Team must be encouraged to maintain practical engagement with the Afghan interim authorities to effectively carry out its mandate on the ground.
messages.Denmark: Denmark welcomes the draft resolution extending the mandate of the Analytical Support and Sanctions Monitoring Team, whose independent reporting remains indispensable. To align the text with the Council's established counter-terrorism framework, we urge the inclusion of standard language reaffirming that all counter-terrorism efforts must strictly comply with international law, including human rights and international humanitarian law. We also encourage the penholder to reflect the gender dimensions of terrorist recruitment and radicalization in the Monitoring Team's reporting tasks.
messages.France: France welcomes the initiative of the United States and fully supports the timely 12-month renewal of the Analytical Support and Sanctions Monitoring Team's mandate under the 1988 regime. Given the persistent and evolving transnational threat posed by ISIL-K and Al-Qaida in and from Afghanistan, preserving the Monitoring Team's analytical and reporting capacities is essential. We ask for the inclusion of the Council's standard language reaffirming that counter-terrorism measures must fully comply with international law, notably international human rights law and international humanitarian law.
messages.Greece: Greece strongly supports the draft resolution and the essential renewal of the Analytical Support and Sanctions Monitoring Team's mandate to counter the growing transnational threat posed by ISIL-K and Al-Qaida. In accordance with established Council practice and our principled foreign policy, we advocate for the inclusion of standard language reaffirming that all counter-terrorism measures must strictly comply with international law, including international human rights law and international humanitarian law. We appreciate the penholder's proactive leadership and constructive engagement on this crucial file.
messages.Guyana: Guyana welcomes the US draft resolution renewing the mandate of the Analytical Support and Sanctions Monitoring Team supporting the 1988 Committee. We strongly support the draft's focus on addressing the threats posed by ISIL-K and Al-Qaida, as well as its clear emphasis on the rights of Afghan women and girls and inclusive governance. Our proposed additions underscore that counter-terrorism efforts must strictly adhere to international humanitarian and human rights law, while preserving humanitarian space in line with resolution 2664 (2022).
messages.Pakistan: Pakistan fully supports the rollover and strengthening of the Analytical Support and Sanctions Monitoring Team's mandate. However, for any text addressing terrorist threats emanating from Afghanistan to be credible and comprehensive, it must explicitly recognize the severe and persistent cross-border threat posed by Tehrik-e Taliban Pakistan (TTP), as consistently documented in the Monitoring Team's own reports. We urge the penholder to reflect TTP alongside ISIL-K and Al-Qaida to ensure the Council addresses all major terrorist threats undermining regional security.
messages.Panama: Panama fully supports the draft resolution circulated by the United States extending the mandate of the Analytical Support and Sanctions Monitoring Team. The Monitoring Team plays an indispensable role in tracking the evolving threats posed by ISIL-K, Al-Qaida, and their affiliates, as well as combating the financing of terrorism and illicit financial flows. We welcome the balanced text and are prepared to vote in favour of the resolution as presented.
messages.Republic of Korea: The Republic of Korea fully supports the draft resolution renewing the mandate of the Analytical Support and Sanctions Monitoring Team for twelve months. Given the persistent and evolving transnational threat posed by terrorist groups operating in and from Afghanistan, particularly ISIL-K and Al-Qaida, the Monitoring Team's independent reporting and technical expertise remain indispensable to the 1988 sanctions regime. We also appreciate the text's clear focus on illicit financing linkages and the continued call for the Taliban to uphold counter-terrorism commitments and human rights, especially for women and girls.
messages.Russian Federation: The Russian Federation supports the rollover of the Monitoring Team's mandate, which is crucial given the persistent transnational menace of ISIL-K. However, it is essential that the resolution explicitly upholds the Monitoring Team's visits to Afghanistan and practical interaction with the de facto authorities as a prerequisite for objective reporting. Additionally, the text should maintain the Council's commitment to review and adjust the 1988 sanctions regime in line with evolving realities on the ground.
messages.Sierra Leone: Sierra Leone welcomes the draft resolution renewing the mandate of the Analytical Support and Sanctions Monitoring Team supporting the 1988 Committee, which remains an essential tool in countering the persistent threats posed by ISIL-K, Al-Qaida, and their affiliates. We strongly support the draft's attention to the nexus between illicit financial flows, transnational crime, and terrorist financing, as well as the protection of fundamental freedoms, particularly for women and girls. We propose a minor addition to operative paragraph 3 to align counter-financing efforts with established international AML/CFT standards, and we stand ready to support the swift adoption of the resolution.
messages.Slovenia: Slovenia strongly supports the twelve-month renewal of the Analytical Support and Sanctions Monitoring Team's mandate and thanks the United States for preparing this draft. In line with our consistent position, we emphasize that all counter-terrorism efforts and sanctions measures must be conducted in strict compliance with international law, particularly international human rights law and international humanitarian law. We also appreciate the retention of strong language on the fundamental rights of Afghan women and girls and look forward to the swift adoption of this resolution.
messages.Somalia: Somalia fully supports the draft resolution renewing the mandate of the Analytical Support and Sanctions Monitoring Team supporting the 1988 Committee. As a country on the frontlines of countering terrorism, we recognize the critical threat posed by groups such as ISIL-K and Al-Qaida and place great value on the Monitoring Team's work in tracking terrorist financing, illicit flows, and transnational networks. We commend the United States for presenting a balanced, substantive text and stand ready to vote in favour.
messages.United Kingdom of Great Britain and Nort: The United Kingdom strongly supports this draft resolution to renew the vital mandate of the Analytical Support and Sanctions Monitoring Team supporting the 1988 Sanctions Committee. We commend the United States for presenting a clear and robust text that highlights the evolving transnational threat posed by ISIL-K and Al-Qaida, while reaffirming the Council's firm expectations regarding the rights of women and girls and counter-terrorism obligations. We stand ready to support the adoption of the resolution as drafted.

steps.summary: As penholder, the United States maintained the text of Revision 1, which commands overwhelming support from Council members. Proposals to confer political recognition on the Taliban, remove gender-focused counter-terrorism analysis, or insert non-consensus designations were rejected to preserve the delicate balance achieved in previous unanimous mandate renewals. The resolution is expected to be adopted unanimously.

before.United States of America:
Thank you, Mr. President.

As the penholder of this draft resolution, the United States is pleased to present this text renewing the mandate of the Analytical Support and Sanctions Monitoring Team supporting the 1988 Sanctions Committee for an additional twelve months. 

The Monitoring Team plays an indispensable role in providing independent, objective, and expert reporting on the evolving terrorist threats emanating from Afghanistan, including from ISIS-K and Al-Qaida, as well as tracking compliance with the 1988 sanctions regime. At a time when terrorist groups continue their efforts to project violence both regionally and globally, ensuring the robust and uninterrupted functioning of the Monitoring Team is essential for international peace and security.

This resolution ensures that the Monitoring Team retains the necessary tools and authority to monitor sanctions implementation, track illicit financing and narcotics trafficking linked to terrorism, and assess transnational threats. We urge all Council members to vote in favor of this resolution. Thank you.

after.Algeria:
Mr. President,

Algeria voted in favour of the resolution just adopted, which renews for twelve months the mandate of the Analytical Support and Sanctions Monitoring Team supporting the 1988 Sanctions Committee. 

Our positive vote reflects Algeria’s unwavering commitment to the fight against terrorism in all its forms and manifestations, as well as our conviction that the 1988 sanctions regime remains an essential instrument in supporting peace, security, and stability in Afghanistan and the wider region. We welcome the Council’s unanimous adoption of this text, which demonstrates the vital importance of maintaining Council unity in addressing common security threats.

We commend the United States, as penholder, for its constructive engagement throughout the consultation process and for taking into account the perspectives of Council members.

Algeria attaches great importance to the work of the Monitoring Team. In this regard, we reiterate that the credibility, legitimacy, and effectiveness of the sanctions regime depend fundamentally on the objective, independent, and non-politicized conduct of the Monitoring Team’s mandate. We also underscore the imperative of preserving the Member State-driven nature of the sanctions listing and delisting processes.

Furthermore, we emphasize the necessity of addressing the multifaceted links between terrorism and transnational organized crime, including the illicit trafficking of narcotics and illegal exploitation of natural resources, which continue to fund terrorist networks. 

Finally, Algeria reaffirms its steadfast commitment to the sovereignty, independence, territorial integrity, and national unity of Afghanistan. As we support counter-terrorism efforts and demand that Afghan territory never again serve as a base or safe haven for terrorist groups such as Da’esh and Al-Qaida, we must also ensure that sanctions measures do not impede humanitarian assistance or aggravate the dire economic and humanitarian conditions faced by the Afghan people.

I thank you.
after.China:
Mr. President,

China welcomes the unanimous adoption of the resolution just put to the vote, extending the mandate of the Analytical Support and Sanctions Monitoring Team supporting the 1988 Sanctions Committee for 12 months. We hope that the Monitoring Team will continue to carry out its work in an objective, impartial, and non-politicized manner, enhance practical engagement and dialogue with the Afghan interim authorities, and provide constructive support to the Committee's work.

I would like to highlight the following points:

First, Afghanistan must not once again become a breeding ground or haven for terrorism. We urge the Afghan interim administration to honor its commitments in good faith, take resolute and decisive measures to combat all terrorist forces—including the Islamic State-Khorasan Province, Al-Qaida, and the East Turkestan Islamic Movement—and prevent its territory from being used by any terrorist group to threaten the security of neighboring countries or the wider international community. In countering terrorism, there should be no double standards, selective approaches, or political instrumentalization.

Secondly, the international community must maintain engagement and dialogue with the Afghan interim authorities in a constructive and pragmatic manner. We encourage the Afghan authorities to build an inclusive and representative political structure, pursue moderate and prudent domestic and foreign policies, and protect the fundamental rights and interests of all people, including women and children. At the same time, the Security Council's sanctions measures under the 1988 regime should be continuously reviewed and adjusted in light of developments on the ground, so as to serve peace, stability, and positive engagement rather than become an obstacle to Afghanistan's normal development and international exchanges.

Thirdly, addressing Afghanistan’s severe economic and humanitarian difficulties remains an urgent task. China has consistently provided assistance within its capacity to support the Afghan people. We urge the countries concerned to immediately and unconditionally return the frozen overseas assets belonging to the Afghan people, lift all unilateral coercive measures, and effectively fulfill their primary responsibilities toward the reconstruction and development of Afghanistan.

China stands ready to continue working with the international community, particularly regional countries, to support Afghanistan in achieving lasting peace, stability, and development, and in smoothly reintegrating into the international family.

Thank you, Mr. President.
after.Denmark:
Mr. President,

Denmark voted in favour of the resolution just adopted, extending the mandate of the Analytical Support and Sanctions Monitoring Team supporting the 1988 Committee.

The Monitoring Team’s independent, objective, and expert reporting is an indispensable tool for the Security Council. It provides us with the necessary factual foundation to evaluate compliance with the 1988 sanctions regime and to understand the evolving terrorist threat landscape. 

Denmark remains deeply concerned by the presence and operational capacity of terrorist groups in Afghanistan, notably ISIL-K and Al-Qaida, which continue to threaten the security of the Afghan people, the region, and the international community as a whole. Afghan territory must never again serve as a base, safe haven, or recruiting ground for terrorists.

At the same time, Denmark firmly underscores that all counter-terrorism measures must strictly adhere to international law, including international human rights law, international refugee law, and international humanitarian law. Effective counter-terrorism and the protection of human rights are mutually reinforcing.

In this context, we recall that enduring peace and stability in Afghanistan cannot be achieved without inclusive governance and the full respect for the human rights and fundamental freedoms of all Afghans. We reiterate our unequivocal call on the Taliban to uphold their obligations and immediately reverse all discriminatory decrees and practices targeting women and girls, whose full, equal, and meaningful participation in public life, education, and employment is essential.

We also welcome the resolution’s focus on the gender dimensions of terrorist recruitment and narratives, as well as the illicit financial flows that sustain these networks.

Denmark thanks the United States as penholder for facilitating this text, and we reaffirm our full support to the 1988 Committee and the Monitoring Team as they carry out their critical mandate.

Thank you.
after.Greece:
Thank you, Mr. President.

Greece welcomed the unanimous adoption of today’s resolution renewing the mandate of the Analytical Support and Sanctions Monitoring Team supporting the 1988 Sanctions Committee for an additional twelve months, and we thank the United States, as penholder, for its efforts in facilitating this consensus.

At a time when terrorist entities, particularly ISIL-K and Al-Qaida, continue to demonstrate dangerous intent and operational capacity to project violence both within the region and globally, the robust and uninterrupted functioning of the Security Council's sanctions architecture remains indispensable. The Monitoring Team plays a vital role through its independent, objective, and evidence-based reporting, providing the Council and the 1988 Committee with the critical assessments necessary to track evolving threats, illicit financial flows, and the nexus between terrorism and transnational organized crime.

Greece reiterates that Afghanistan must never again become a safe haven or platform for international terrorism, in line with resolution 2593 (2021). We urge the Taliban to fulfill their counter-terrorism commitments unequivocally and to address the presence of terrorist groups operating on Afghan soil.

At the same time, lasting peace and stability in Afghanistan cannot be achieved without the full respect for international law, including human rights law and international humanitarian law. We reiterate our deep concern over the ongoing systematic erosion of the rights and fundamental freedoms of Afghan women and girls, and we call for their full, equal, and meaningful participation in all aspects of public life, alongside the establishment of an inclusive and representative system of governance.

Greece remains fully committed to supporting the 1988 sanctions regime and all collective international efforts to eliminate the scourge of terrorism in all its forms and manifestations.

Thank you, Mr. President.
after.Pakistan:
Mr. President,

Pakistan voted in favour of the resolution just adopted, extending the mandate of the Analytical Support and Sanctions Monitoring Team supporting the 1988 Sanctions Committee for another year. We thank the United States, as the penholder, for its efforts in facilitating this consensus text.

As an immediate neighbour that has borne the heaviest brunt of terrorism over the past several decades, losing more than 80,000 precious lives and suffering hundreds of billions of dollars in economic losses, Pakistan attaches the highest importance to peace, security, and stability in Afghanistan and our wider region.

The reports of the Monitoring Team have consistently provided valuable, independent, and evidence-based assessments regarding the presence, operations, and evolving threat of terrorist entities operating in and from Afghanistan. Today, the most severe and immediate threat to Pakistan emanates from terrorist groups operating with impunity from Afghan territory, foremost among them the Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP)—the *Fitna al-Khawarij*—alongside Da’esh-Khorasan (ISIL-K), Al-Qaida, and other affiliated terrorist networks and regional proxies. These groups continue to acquire sophisticated weaponry left behind after the foreign troop withdrawal and carry out cross-border attacks killing Pakistani civilians and security personnel.

We reiterate that the Afghan interim authorities must fulfill their international commitments, including those explicitly reaffirmed in resolution 2593 (2021). The territory of Afghanistan must never be permitted to be used as a base, safe haven, or logistical hub to threaten or attack any country, or to recruit, shelter, or train terrorists. Effective, decisive, and verifiable action against all terrorist organizations without distinction is not only an international obligation, but a strategic prerequisite for the long-term peace and stability of Afghanistan and the region.

At the same time, Pakistan remains firmly committed to the welfare and wellbeing of the brotherly Afghan people. We continue to advocate for sustained, constructive engagement with the Afghan authorities, the unhindered provision of humanitarian aid, and the revival of Afghanistan’s economy. A stable, economically viable Afghanistan, at peace with itself and its neighbours, respecting fundamental human rights—including the rights of women and girls to education and employment—and established upon inclusive governance, serves the common interest of the entire international community.

Pakistan stands ready to continue working closely with the 1988 Committee, the Monitoring Team, and international partners to combat terrorism in all its forms and manifestations, and to support collective efforts toward enduring peace in Afghanistan.

I thank you.
after.Republic of Korea:
Mr. President,

The Republic of Korea voted in favor of the resolution just adopted, which extends the mandate of the Analytical Support and Sanctions Monitoring Team supporting the 1988 Sanctions Committee for another year. We thank the United States, as the penholder, for its efforts in steering this process to a unanimous outcome.

Today’s unanimous adoption sends a clear and united message: the Security Council remains firmly committed to countering terrorism in all its forms and manifestations and ensuring that Afghanistan never again serves as a safe haven or springboard for international terrorism.

The threat posed by terrorist groups operating in and from Afghanistan, particularly ISIL-K and Al-Qaida, remains grave and concerning. As recent high-impact attacks and foiled plots across multiple regions have tragically demonstrated, the transnational operational reach and ambitions of ISIL-K continue to pose severe threats to regional and international peace and security. In this context, the independent, objective, and evidence-based reporting provided by the Monitoring Team is vital. Their comprehensive assessments—tracking terrorist recruitment, operational networks, and the illicit financial nexus, including narcotics trafficking—are indispensable to the effective implementation and integrity of the 1988 sanctions regime.

We once again call upon the Taliban to adhere strictly to their counter-terrorism commitments under relevant Security Council resolutions, including resolution 2593 (2021). Furthermore, enduring peace and stability in Afghanistan cannot be decoupled from respect for the human rights and fundamental freedoms of all Afghans, particularly the rights of women and girls to education, employment, and public life, as well as the establishment of an inclusive and representative governance system.

In conclusion, as the Republic of Korea concludes its term on the Security Council, we reaffirm our unwavering commitment to multilateral cooperation in global counter-terrorism efforts and full support for the vital work of the Monitoring Team and the 1988 Sanctions Committee.

Thank you, Mr. President.
after.Russian Federation:
Mr. President,

The Russian Federation voted in favour of the resolution extending the mandate of the Analytical Support and Sanctions Monitoring Team supporting the 1267/1988 Committees for another twelve months.

Our consistent position is that the expert work of the Monitoring Team is essential for the effective functioning of the 1988 Sanctions Committee. We have always advocated for preserving the operational capacity of this body through a pragmatic, non-politicized approach, and we appreciate the penholder’s efforts to ensure a timely extension of its mandate.

At the same time, we would like once again to underscore that the effectiveness and credibility of the Monitoring Team’s reports directly depend on its ability to maintain direct, practical engagement with the de facto authorities in Kabul. Visits by the experts to Afghanistan and dialogue with relevant interlocutors on the ground remain an indispensable condition for obtaining objective, verifiable, and balanced information, rather than relying on unverified external claims or politically motivated assessments.

We must realistically assess the security situation in Afghanistan and the wider region. The primary terrorist threat remains the regional branch of the Islamic State—ISIL-Khorasan—which continues its subversive activities, seeking to destabilize both Afghanistan and its neighbors, while projecting terror across the globe, as we have tragically witnessed firsthand. The de facto authorities are waging an active struggle against this threat, and the international community should encourage, not undermine, practical counter-terrorism cooperation with regional states to eradicate the terrorist menace emanating from ISIL-K and its affiliates.

Furthermore, we reiterate that the sanctions regime under resolution 1988 (2011) was established in a completely different political reality and must not be treated as a permanent punitive instrument. The Security Council must objectively review the restrictions and make necessary, timely adjustments to the sanctions measures to reflect the evolving realities on the ground, facilitate Afghanistan’s socioeconomic recovery, and support broader peace and stabilization efforts. Addressing the dire humanitarian and economic crisis in Afghanistan also requires the immediate and unconditional return of Afghanistan’s national reserves, which remain unlawfully frozen by Western nations.

Russia remains committed to constructive, coordinated efforts within the Council and with regional partners in support of a peaceful, stable, and independent Afghanistan, free from terrorism and drug-related crime.

Thank you.
after.Sierra Leone:
Mr. President,

Sierra Leone welcomes the unanimous adoption of the resolution extending the mandate of the Analytical Support and Sanctions Monitoring Team assisting the 1988 Sanctions Committee for a period of twelve months. We thank the United States, as the penholder, for its constructive leadership throughout the negotiation process.

Our vote in favour reflects Sierra Leone’s firm and consistent commitment to multilateral efforts to combat terrorism in all its forms and manifestations. The 1988 sanctions regime and the vital, independent work of the Analytical Support and Sanctions Monitoring Team remain indispensable instruments for promoting peace, security, and stability in Afghanistan and preventing the country from once again serving as a platform or safe haven for terrorist groups.

Sierra Leone remains deeply concerned by the persistent presence and operational capacity of terrorist groups in Afghanistan, notably ISIL-K and Al-Qaida, and their ability to plan and carry out attacks with regional and global repercussions. We also underscore the critical importance of disrupting the nexus between terrorism financing, the illicit trafficking of narcotics, and the illegal exploitation of natural resources. In this regard, we welcome the emphasis placed on strengthening international cooperation to combat illicit financial flows and adherence to international anti-money laundering and counter-terrorist financing standards.

Furthermore, we recall that counter-terrorism efforts must strictly adhere to international law, including international human rights law and international humanitarian law. We reiterate our call for the protection of fundamental freedoms and human rights in Afghanistan, particularly the rights of women and girls to education, employment, and full participation in public life.

In conclusion, Sierra Leone reaffirms its full support for the work of the 1988 Committee and the Monitoring Team, and we remain dedicated to collaborating with all Council members to advance lasting peace, security, and stability in Afghanistan and the wider region.

I thank you.
